utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. May we have appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jim Cowles and I'm here representing the Prosecution along with Mr. George Huber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Edina Residovic and I appear on behalf of Delalic, and the co-counsel is Mr. O'Sullivan from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Tomisalv Kuzmanovic on behalf of Mr. Mucic. Mr. Olujic will be here later today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic. I appear on behalf of Hazim Delic and the co-counsel is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey, I represent Esad Landzo, along with Nancy Boler and Mr. Calvin Saunders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. McMurrey, we're expecting you to lead your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have an announcement to make that the witness is not available until 2.30 this afternoon. I'm asking that the Court please show tolerance and indulgence for this problem and we'd like to begin presenting evidence at 2.30 this afternoon, if the Court could please allow the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it still one of the witnesses you're expecting, or another strange witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, it's not a strange witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you now telling the Trial Chamber you cannot lead evidence until 2.30 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's what I'm informing the Court of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I hope that is a firm time when we can expect you to lead your witness, not when we come at that time we have another story. I don't call it a fairy story, because I've not even heard the story. So, we hope at 2.30 you will start with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will begin testimony at 2.30, exactly as I have represented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't you think we have wasted enough time already?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We've given indulgence after indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, you have been very tolerant and very indulgent through the whole Defence case, I believe, and through the Prosecution case, as far as that goes, the Court has shown great understanding for the problems associated with the witnesses we have tried to bring here. And you're absolutely right, Judge Jan, you have all been very tolerant about this. I was just asking the Court to allow just two and a half more hours of court time and then we will be wrapping up our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. We will rise again and with the concession of other counsel, we'll rise and come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Karabdic is ill this afternoon and he has asked me to carry on in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving us that information. Now, Mrs. McMurrey. Let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the Defence of Esad Landzo calls Esad Landzo to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: May the Prosecution be heard, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to this. We were not informed that the defendant would testify. We've never received any written notice. I even asked the Defence counsel this morning who would be the witness this afternoon and they refused to inform the Prosecution. I realise we can probably not prevent him from testifying. However, since we've not had the seven days' notice as required and as we fully complied with, we have not been adequately informed. We will, therefore, if Your Honours allow the defendant to testify, we would then request a brief recess or a short break following his testimony before we commence cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: At least that's the first things that lead you, whether it will be necessary to cross-examine. You have any necessity to cross-examine, then the Trial Chamber will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Excuse me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: An accused is always a competent witness at his own trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I fully understand that. However, in compliance with the Trial Chamber's rulings, we have never been informed that he would be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I understand that, thank you. Please let him come to the stand. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ESAD LANDZO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please sit down. You may proceed, Mrs. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Landzo, Esad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I know, Mr. Landzo, that you have learned to speak English, but you prefer to testify in your native language today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Court the reason that you have made this last minute decision to testify in this Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason is that all my witnesses and witnesses in fact that were supposed to submit their testimonies, refused for a reason unknown to me to come here and to tell their truth. This is why I decided to tell you what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were they witnesses who had agreed to come at one time, but changed their mind right before they came to The Hague; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what they told to my Defence counsels who had talked to them some 7 -- 14 days ago. They had said that they would come, that they were willing to come, but at the last minute they stated that they would not like to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, did you want to testify before the Trial Chamber before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the very beginning when I arrived in The Hague, I asked for Mr. Brackovic, my first Defence counsel to allow me to tell the truth because I do not have a habit of lie, but he had told me for a reason unknown to me that that was not a good idea, that I should not do it and he advised me that I should use other modes to deny all the counts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you make an attempt to talk to the Prosecutor even as recently as last summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the time when Mr. Ackerman was my lead Defence counsel, I asked him to establish a contact with a Prosecutor to be able to talk to him, but only Mrs. McMurrey talked to him without his consent, so I couldn't talk to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you have any concerns for your family before you were testifying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much and I would like to thank their honours for the patience they have exuded and manifested while allowing my sister to come here and allowing her to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, I want to go on to the evidence that we'd like to present before the Court. Can you give a description of what you were like as a young boy before you started primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, generally, before the war, I was a peaceful person. I was a person that didn't like to be in company, in a large group. I tended to spend most of my time on my own and with animals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am talking about as a young boy, before you started primary school, what kind of child were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, generally, I was a sickly child. I had a congenital bronchitis that later on developed into asthma. As far as I can recall and as far as I was told by my mother, I was a very sick person. I tended to play on my own instead of playing with my brothers. I was different from the others, as far as I can recall and as far as my mother told me, I was always different from the rest of the children. I was sickly, I would very often go to the hospital because of my breathing difficulties. And I would avoid, for reasons that I do not know, a large group of children. I would not play with my brothers as often as I had played on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you consider yourself as a shy child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very. Even at school I was such and many of my teachers would ask me why I was such a person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court about one time when you were a young boy and you had an incident with some goats, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, my parents lived in a suburban area of Konjic and a neighbour of mine had young goats that I was very much afraid of. One day, they playing probably would run after me. I was afraid that they would push me with their horns, therefore, and I fell and they would really push me over and roll me over. For months after that I would twitch with my eyes and the doctor that examined me had told my parents that they would be, they would have to be kind of nice to me so that I would lose this fear. And the twitching of the eyes had discontinued afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, what age were you when you started primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you the same size as the other children in school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. I was one of the smallest in my class.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you have very many friends in primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except a relative of mine who I would hang around with mostly, even though I spent four years with the same pupils in my class, they remained sort of strangers from me, so I would either be on my own or I would spend my time with this relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you have a talent that you didn't know about until you were in primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 4th grade of the primary school, I entered the painting club and at that time I sort of discovered my talent for drawing and painting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you have a special teacher that encouraged you in that field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Vera Bratic was the teacher. She was my teacher of arts from the 5th grade to the 8th grade of the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What ethnic background was she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I have no idea at that time. But, later, when the war started, I learned that she was a Serb and even her husband was a member of the command that I had belonged of. He was, in fact, one of the territory defence command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So he was a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you consider Ms. Bratic one of your closest friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The only person at school and outside the school, apart from my parents that I had trusted, that I could confide in. She would always listen to me. She would always encourage me to go on with my painting, to learn and to get good grades at school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did the other children ask you to draw pictures for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at school and on the alley where I lived, everywhere, except the smaller children who want wanted me to draw pictures on their T-shirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you ever asked by your classmates to join them to do things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only subject where they asked me to join, to do something for them, was the arts class because I was one of the best among all students at school. So this is when they communicated with me, otherwise, they would distance themselves from me. They probably consider me to be different and not belonging, but as far as painting and drawing is concerned, here it was a different story.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you come from a poor family, a middle-class family, a wealthy family? What kind of family did you come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came from a family of, a large family of several members, seven members. I couldn't say we were a rich family. My father was the only parent working. So somewhere around the lower middle-class family. We were not really poor, we could get along.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were there seven people living in a one bedroom apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when your grandmother was living with you, how many people lived in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you have one friend named Valentin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the time from the 5th to the 8th grade of the primary school and we continued being friends in the secondary school all the way until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you say that you were close to your parents during that time of your life?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to interpose an objection, at this point to the relevancy of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might respond. It all adds up and goes to the mental state and the personality disorders that we claim in the defence of diminished mental responsibility and that's the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you close to your parents in primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout this time, particularly close to my mother because she would spend all her time with us, with children, and I would -- she would help me with my homework during the primary school. She would check on my grades. She was in charge of everything while my father was working and he would spend his free time resting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go to secondary school. Before you went to secondary school, did you apply to be accepted to a different secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Upon graduation from the primary school and upon proposal, or rather, suggestion by my former teacher of the primary school, Vera Bratic, I applied to the secondary art school in Sarajevo. I passed the entrance exam, but because of the lack of financial funds, since my father was the only breadwinner and there were four children to be schooled, I had to enter the Konjic Secondary School. I decided to enroll in that school and to graduate from there just to get the diploma, otherwise, I was not really interested in the type of school. I couldn't go to the school of my choice, so I choose this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And so when you were denied the ability to go to art school, how did you feel? How did that affect you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Angry, particularly angry with my father because I blamed him, although I shouldn't have, but I blamed him for not allowing me to do it. Actually, I withdrew even more within myself, avoiding contact with other children, talking to other children about this. I particularly was reluctant to talk to my classmates who enrolled in military school. I just didn't want to talk about something that was an indication of the future, of my future. So, in a way, I was ashamed and I blamed my father, although, subsequently, I realised that there was no reason for blaming him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you were forced to go to a secondary school in Konjic. And, what was that specialisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't forced, I could just not continue education, but I wanted to continue with education to finish a secondary school and to, perhaps, through my own financial resources, finance myself through an art school afterwards, so I enrolled in Konjic, the secondary school, woodworking secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And how did that woodworking secondary school affect your asthma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere from the second grade of this secondary school we had practical exercises where we had to go to a workshop in a company, processing wood. My father was employed there too. So we would get into contact with machines. We would work on the wood. There was lots of sawdust because, obviously, we would be working on woods and very often I had to stay at home because of the breathing problems. And, at the end, I just passed the test without following the classes on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you graduated from secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, after you graduated from secondary school, what happened to you immediately after that? Did you -- could you find a job then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was an unfortunate time, not only for me, but for the whole country, the former Yugoslavia, which was in a crisis as far as money was concerned. So it was very difficult at that time to get a job, particularly for us, the younger people, even those who were employed in factories would not -- they would not get their salaries on a regular basis. So I would just go to the student service. I would work for a day or two, for an hour or two, to earn my pocket money. It was really very difficult and I couldn't really get a job at that time. I couldn't work over a longer period of time, of course, because of my health problems, but I worked as much as I could to help out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you end up hanging out with your brother and his friends during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I started hanging around with them after the completion of the second grade of the secondary school. My brother left for the military service at that time and in a way I started hanging around this company. These had, namely, been people that I knew a little better than the others. Although some of them were older. Some of them were two, three, five years older them me. I would hang around with this group of people. Well, maybe I could have found better company, but I had always been afraid of new friends, new friendships, of new people, so I preferred this company. Well, I just knew them and I would hang around with them because these were the friends of my brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, did these friends of your brothers take advantage of you in a way any time you had spending money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I can understand this, but at that time I couldn't. For example, when, sometimes, I would get some pocket money from my father or I would earn some money on my own, I would buy alcohol for them. I would buy drinks and then when I was hanging around, they would send me to fetch something for them, go there, bring us that. Go there, fetch this, because I was the youngest and whatever they needed they would just send me to fetch it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you do whatever they asked you to do to try and win approval in that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It would happen that, for example, I would go to a store to fetch drinks. I would not find it there and I would have to go to another store, to ten stores sometimes because I wasn't allowed to get back without the drink. At that time, I thought I had to do it for them. Now I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Talking about the alcohol and pills, I want to jump ahead a little bit. In 1996, you told some health experts, mental health experts about alcohol and pills, why did you tell that story then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon the suggestion of Mr. Brackovic, the then Defence counsel of mine, he asked me, actually he insisted, that I tell the story, that I took alcohol and pills. Because, for him, that was a way of defending me, claiming that I was beyond self-control. I didn't know what I was really doing. I don't know anything about these legal matters, but that was the basis of his defence. And having followed his suggestion, I made this testimony and I had repeated this testimony to a number of doctors and experts who examined me, even though this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to move on to a person who lived in your building. Can you tell us about a man named Ibo or Ibro and how you felt about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hamid Peliba (phoen) was my neighbour for practically 18 years. He lived the floor above ours. I knew him for 18 years. When I was a small child, he was a good man, not only to me, but to all the children on the alley. He would tend to protect us from certain acts, particularly when my mother started baby-sitting for his son, Arman. My mother told him that she would not allow me to hang around with my brothers' friends any more because they were drinking, taking pills. And, in a way, he wanted to protect me. When he would come across me, together with these youngsters, he would smack me and he immediately sent me home. He would check whether I arrived home. So he tried to bring me away from this company, from these so-called friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And how did you feel about Ibro? Did you care about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much. I highly respected him as an elderly person. A person I knew for 18 years, from a neighbour of mine. And he had many nice gestures towards me. And no reason to hate anyone if he does good to you. And I liked him as a neighbour, as a person who protected me against bad influence and as a neighbour, as an older person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, in early 1991, what happened to the fingers of your right hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know why I became quarrelling with my father, but that was in 1991, when I couldn't attend the art school. And after this impossibility of attending the school, I was to -- I blamed everything, my father for everything. And then we quarrelled, the two of us. And simply, I became nervous and I grabbed something I found in a cupboard, a knife. I really don't know why I grabbed that knife. And I hit against this cupboard and on that occasion I slipped and I cut four fingers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you never had any intention of using that knife on your father, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you cut your fingers, what was the result of that injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 5th has been cut down to the bones of the 5th finger. I could see the tendons and the bones. The second and the third fingers were cut less deeply. And the others, that one was really very severely cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you end up in the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, immediately a neighbour, a Serb, a Serbian neighbour took me to the hospital with her car, where they bandaged it and told me to contact Dr. Buturovic the next morning who would operate on my fingers. That is, in fact, what I did the next morning. My elder brother accompanied me to the hospital the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And was Dr. Buturovic able to repair your tendons in your fingers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he succeeded, but I know what he did to me. Through the 4th and the 5th finger, he pulled a thread through it, with which I would then do exercises and the 4th and the 5th today are bent and stiff, even the third one is damaged. I really don't know whether it's due to the lack of a professional approach of his or maybe I didn't do enough of exercises or I was supposed to be treated further. But I am handicapped in the second right hand. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could you hold your hand up so the Trial Chamber can see how it's positioned now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And is that the way your hand has been since 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you miss school because of this injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was still going to school at the time, and after that, after the operation I spent five days in the hospital. After that I was absent from school for some time, and I had to make up and take additional tests in order to pass that grade. I was also, did not have to attend gym classes. Sometimes I did attend them, but I had pain, and then the teacher would let me go to the hospital and get a pain killer injection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This hand injury, did you still graduate from high school with it, I mean from secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Although, gym and for the professional subjects I received just passing marks in order to be able to graduate, but physically I couldn't take the tests for these two subjects. I couldn't create a piece, work a piece of wood on a machine, and I couldn't do gym. So I just received passing marks in these two subjects, otherwise I had average marks and in order not to fail they gave me passing marks. That was after my injury, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: With this deformity in your hand, did it embarrass you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, up until the beginning of the war I always shook hands with my left hand. And many asked why I was shaking hands with my left hand, or why did I hold my right hand in my pocket. And I always had it in wintertime wrapped up. And I always shook hands with the left, many didn't know why. Many people who know me a long time didn't know about this injury. I tried to conceal that. I was a bit ashamed. Everybody was normal except me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, when you graduated from high school and you couldn't find a job then, how were you feeling emotionally at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, emotionally I felt very poorly. Not only emotionally, if you don't have a future and you're young, you've finished school and you see no future in it at all, then you have no will to live, not even for the next day, not to speak of the next year. It seemed as if all my ships had sunk. That wasn't only my case, but also for many of my generation, because it's a period when you should be creating your own future and there were no possibilities of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just in a few words, looking back on that period in 1991, '92, can you explain what kind of personality you had before the war in Croatia and Konjic, if you can come up with words to describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I describe psychologically, or personality?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Personality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it, maybe it would be a question which ought to be put to somebody else, but I'll try to explain. I always wished to satisfy others, particularly satisfy the older people. And I liked playing with children, with younger people. I played with animals. So, as I can say for myself, as far as I can say, I was a model for younger children, a model for younger ones. That was before the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, in March did you receive a notice to do your JNA service sometime in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the month. I remember receiving the call up papers that I must contact the office in Mostar and not in Konjic, because the JNA collected all the communal, the municipal documentation for the younger generations. I received the call up papers, and the Muslims and Croats, it was in their interest, it wasn't in their interest to fight on that side within the JNA. The JNA was fighting in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did your father tell you not to follow up with the JNA service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my father and many of my acquaintances who received the call up papers also turned down, and it was on the advice of my father, mostly at his advice I turned that down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what did he recommend that you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To hide. He actually suggested to me to hide with my uncle, so at his place some 30 kilometres away from Konjic. And there was always the possibility to hide there should the military police show up, because in Konjic you would have MP patrols on a daily basis and they would try to hunt down the conscripts, and should they find you they would, of course, bring you in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you be arrested if you didn't fulfil your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And so, what did you do as a result of that? When you said you went into hiding, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really couldn't say that I was hiding. I had some friends from the school, Cipetic was the surname, and I worked with him at Miro's. We knew each other a bit better, and he proposed, he told me that he has a brother in Rijeka in Croatia and that we could move there because Rijeka is very far from the front lines in Croatia. And with the help of that brother we could find a job and after that, that we could move on. We decided to go there. And I told my parents that I would be visiting my grandparents for 20 or 30 days and that I would be back and after this trouble is over.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And was this in April or May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, I know it was the beginning of summer. I remember some very warm days. It was very, very hot. It must have been that period, but I cannot tell you exactly. I know it was the beginning of the warm season, and the area of Herzegovina, these warm periods begin quite early. Not like in Bosnia, you have two regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina; Herzegovina was always warmer than Bosnia and the warm days began sooner in Herzegovina than Bosnia, that was that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, when you left Konjic when your friend Cipeta where did you go and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time we talked about it he told me he knows of a man who will be, who goes to Croatia regularly, and that his brother would pay him when we, once we arrived Rijeka for the trip. And we left Konjic at dusk. And then we moved through Jablanica, it was already dark. And then we moved on to Mecandum (Phoen) Road, we couldn't continue along the asphalt road to Mostar because the JNA was present there, and they were arresting the young people who were at the military age. So, we went along, I didn't know exactly where we were going, and I didn't know exactly which area this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around midnight we stopped in a village, and since this was a pickup van, and as far as I could see from the lights, there were stone houses, I believed we were either in Dalmatia or Herzegovina, because only in these areas do you have such stone houses. Here we stopped. The driver took us to the home owner, and he told us to sleep over there, that this home owner would then see to it that we continued our trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say the driver, are you talking about your friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the person who drove us from Konjic to this village. I don't know, I didn't know this person. They had the licence plates from Konjic, but I don't know whether the man was from Konjic. It was the first and the last time I saw the man who drove us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was he a friend of your friend Cipeta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Cipetic told me that he knows somebody who could take us, but I don't know whether they were friends, because they didn't talk between each other while we were travelling. I don't know whether they were friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you stay in this stranger's home that evening in this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were offered dinner and we slept there, and at his advice, he took us, we saw that this was either Dalmatia or Herzegovina, because these were all stone houses and it was a stony area, very stony, very -- and we believed it was either Herzegovina or Dalmatia, he took us to the other part of the village and a long house, like.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are you talking about that night? Did you sleep there and did you get up the next day and that's when he took you to another part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the morning. After sleeping the next morning he took us to this long house, and we were, while we were entering we saw some uniformed men in black uniforms, and when we entered that building, he brought us to some rooms like classrooms. We entered and there was a man sitting there, an officer, a person in a uniform. He didn't introduce himself. We told him our names, he offered us a seat, he asked us who we are, where we're going, the basic information. After that, when we told him, he offered us something like forms to fill in with our names, surnames, dates of birth, whether we served the JNA or not, and when we said no, we didn't, and that we were fleeing from that service and that we don't want to take part in the armed forces, he said in a rather unkind tone, "Well, you cannot go there prior to getting your training." So, we had really no choice. We couldn't go there where we intended, and we couldn't go back, because we had no transportation. So we had to stay in that village and go through that form of training.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say you couldn't go there, they said that you couldn't go to Croatia without participating in training first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was one. And we didn't know the place, we didn't know where we were. We didn't know where to go. We practically had no choice. There where we were, we had to stay, because you didn't know what you could expect behind the next curve, whether the JNA, an armed unit. So, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you stayed there, did they take you to some kind of barracks and give you a place to sleep? Or what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We slept in that building where they had their offices. We had a room where we slept that, myself, Cipeta, and we found some other five, six young men. And from their stories we heard they were from central Bosnia, that they wanted to go to Croatia, that they were from central Bosnia, and we spent there some 15, 20 days. And we were trained to use our weapons, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was going to ask you what kind of training you received, and were there many soldiers there, or a few soldiers there? How many people were there at this training facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was a training centre, but they had, their unit had a temporary base. It was the house, a unit, had a temporary base. And they were fighting somewhere in Croatia near Cazin (Phoen) Zadar and there they had come to this area for a rest. I understood that the Croatian border was quite near; but otherwise Herzegovina was always a safe haven for those who were not former Yugoslavia and for all anti-Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say HOS and you talk about black uniforms, are those different from HVO and the regular Croatian uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were black uniforms, completely black. But you had also representatives from the HVO from the Bosnian army who had later on black uniforms; but they wore exclusively black uniforms, they were called the Black Shirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In early 1991, or April or May of 1991, were these considered paramilitary groups, or regular army at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the views of the Serbs. For example, even the regulars of the Croatian army were considered paramilitary; while Croatia, after its independence, considered the JNA paramilitary. And thus, also the HVO was considered at a certain time as paramilitary. A general of the house was in fact killed by a member of the HVO in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, can you go on and describe the training that you received at this military camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first 15, 20 days we went through the normal training, we were given some old uniforms of different colours, M-48, old rifles that we used to learn how to shoot, to put the rifles together, to take apart. Later on we, for some five, six days, went to the political courses, as they called it. We were brought to a room that resembled a classroom, we were sitting in a circle and they would bring some civilians in. We were told that they are Serbs, that they had participated in the battles. There were also women, there were uniformed men. And they showed us, using them, how to do certain things. They would bring these people in and the trainer would come from the back to demonstrate to us how to, in fact, kill somebody from behind, like a sentry guard, using a knife. And we would have to sit around and observe this demonstration. Later we were told to hold these individuals, you know, they were drunk. They would bring a person in, we would have to hold these individuals, and they will stab these individuals with a metal object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say these individuals, was it one person, two persons, three persons? Did they do them all at one time, did they do them individually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were three, four of them who would lecture us, who would provide the so-called lectures. Two were practically showing us how to do it while the others would show us TV tapes, photographs of burned down villages, of killed women and children, telling us that this happened to the Croatians in Croatia and this would also happen to the Bosnians in Bosnia, unless we would get ready on time. They called themselves Chetniks, and they said Chetniks are ready to start the march, just like in 1941 to slaughter the Muslims, and particularly the Croats. So, these videotapes and photographs would be shown to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you talk about these people appeared drunk, were they drunk or were they drugged by someone or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once or twice they were drunk. When they would demonstrate to us how to use a knife, they were drunk, indeed, once or twice. On other occasions with others, I don't know, I couldn't notice whether they were drunk. Maybe they were under the influence of drugs or something. But I don't know that. They looked normal, they moved in a normal manner. I couldn't notice it. But on these two occasions, they were indeed drunk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say they were drunk, are you talking about the soldiers training you were drunk or the subjects that they brought in were drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two trainers who were demonstrating, these two soldiers that would demonstrate how to do it, they were drunk. Not the person that was brought in, but rather those individuals who were demonstrating to us how to do it, they were drunk, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about this demonstration, was this an actual training for you that you had to participate in, or was it something that you merely were supposed to watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First we watched and then on one occasion when they were using a metal saw, cutting off one person's fingers, I had to hold this person, he was kneeling down, his head was put on a chair, we had to hold his hands on his back so he couldn't get up while they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And how many days did have you to be subjected to this kind of training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five, six, maybe a day, give and take a day, but somewhere around five, six days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And how did you feel at that time? What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw my grandmother die, but that was of natural death and that was the only person in my life that I saw dead. Now, you come to a place where you see people dying of force, use of force and not natural death, you really are shocked. We couldn't sleep. We would ask a doctor to give us sleeping pills. There were many psychological problems. Whenever you would close your eyes, the pictures from the past day would come back to you. You would get up during the night, you would walk around, you would have one pill, this wouldn't help, and then you would get another pill, but you had to take the pills in order to fall asleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you and your friend Cipeta, were you afraid at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. For example, they would come in drunk, and you would know. Later we were told who these people were, and when you walk up and down the room, you don't know whether they will turn the rifle at you and shoot, because they would shoot up in the air, they would shoot around, you have come to this place and you didn't know what could happen, and it could very well happen that the next day I would be taken into that room and used for demonstration, you couldn't go anywhere, you had no choice, had you to stay there. And simply we really didn't feel very safe. I didn't feel safe. I don't know what the others felt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: How old were you and Cipeta at this time in April, May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 18, I think. Around 18 years, both of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when did you turn 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March, 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you could say you were barely 18 then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, how did you, how were you able to leave this training facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 25, 30 days, at most, that was the period, 25 to 30 days, we were called up to go back to the office to the commander who would congratulate us on having completed the training, telling us that we would be able to go to Croatia, but not where we wanted to go, but to the military units in Croatia, where the HOS or some other, we were told that we would have to join the military units, or to go back home. This was the choice we were given, both me and Cipeta opted for return to home, because we didn't want to go to any military forces. We would have joined the JNA had we wanted to serve in the army, where we perhaps would have or wouldn't have gone through such horrors, taking into account what the JNA was doing in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So when you decided that you both wanted to go home, did you turn in your uniform and your gun then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had -- a pistol, I had a gun, yes, I turned it in, and a convoy of some ten trucks, I assumed that these were trucks that were, that had brought in weapons, well, they put us on one of these trucks, took us to Jablanica and from Jablanica we were then transferred today Konjic. Because these trucks then continued from Jablanica towards Prozor or some other place. We just used them to get to Jablanica and then we would continue to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: These trucks, were they HVO trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. These were civilian trucks, not military trucks. They were actually wooden trucks belonging to a company. We didn't really sit next to the drivers. We didn't ask the drivers a lot. I was not really interested in these details, I just wanted to get home.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you got home, what happened then? What did you do when you got home to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before leaving Cipeta was working for Elmir Hadzialic, for Miro, everybody called him Miro. And upon our return, I spent a few days at home walking around the town, not knowing what to do. I felt the need to tell my story to somebody, but I was afraid that people would consider me crazy, because at that time the war hadn't started, and should I start telling somebody the story, they would consider me crazy, this was not possible, this was unfeasable for that time. So I would spend a few days in the town and then Cipeta called me to help him to do something at Miro's, which I did, and then I stayed working for Miro until the outbreak of the war. That was about, well, I worked for Miro somewhere for ten, eleven months, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would that have been possibly in the month of June or July that you started working for Miro? When would that be, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly at the end of June, the end of June that I started. Or perhaps the beginning of July. I really don't know. I don't know exactly, but I know it was summer, the children would go and swim, but I had to go and work. I worked with Miro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, had you worked for Miro briefly before you and Cipeta left Konjic, or had you never worked for him before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back, that was the first time I started working for Miro. Upon my return, when Cipeta asked me to help him to do something for Miro, then I stayed and continued working for Miro upon Cipeta's recommendation. He recommended me to Miro and Miro accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what was your working arrangement with Miro? What did you do and how were you compensated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did everything he asked me to do, and since this was a very difficult period of time, there were certain vouchers used, and not money, real money, so, vouchers, could be used only to buy in certain shops. I decided not to use these vouchers, but to accept food and clothes as compensation. I would take these home for my parents for my brothers. So, it was not compensation in money, but in kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what kind of work did you do for Miro exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything he asked me to do. That was either working in a shop as a shop assistant. In a warehouse, checking the goods, keeping records of everything that was stored in the warehouse. Sometimes I would go together with Miro to fetch goods to other parts of the town. Cipeta would go with him to distant places such as Sarajevo, Zagreb, et cetera. I would sometimes go with Miro also to Zenica to Tuzla. I would load and unload goods. I would work in Miro's father's house. When I finished my work with Miro, if his father needed anything, I would go and help him 24 hours a day for a week or two weeks. I would not even go home to sleep. I would stay there. I would work as a night guard. I would walk around and in front of the shop watching the goods because goods had to be left in front of the store. There was no room in the warehouse, so I would spend nights outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Where would you sleep when you stayed on the property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Miro's office. Me and Cipeta, we would sometimes sleep together or in turns. If Cipeta had to go home, he would go home, I would stay. Where I would go home, Cipeta would stay. But, basically, we mainly slept together. Because sometimes in the morning at 5.00 a.m. the truck would arrive, everything had to be ready for transportation. So we had to be there round the clock, available all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say you loaded and unloaded, did Cipeta help you? Did you ever unload anything very heavy by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cipeta and me, we unloaded small trucks, a truck of 5 to 6 tons capacity. When larger trucks would an arrive, we would ask people to help us and we would pay them to help us with unloading. We would have five, six sometimes ten people when two trucks would arrive at a time, that would work. And my job primarily was to push the goods towards the truck. Not load or unload, push the goods, so that the person who would load or unload on the truck would do it. And I would also help Cipeta with the stock taking of the goods that arrived due to my injuries, Cipeta was familiar with, he was sort of a boss to me. He was older than me, so I followed Miro's orders and then Cipeta's.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What was your relationship with Miro. Did you have a good relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He called Cipeta and me brothers, not workers, brothers. And we also called him "brother". He was more of a friend than a boss. Everything we asked him he did for us. Everything he asked from us, we would do. So it was really genuine friendship. It was a friendly relationship and not one of boss and an employee.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And would you say that you did things up and above the call of duty? I mean, besides your job description, did you do other things for Miro too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I -- my working time was from 7.00 a.m. to 8.00 p.m. After 8.00 p.m., I could say, sorry, my time is up, but, of course, I worked for him. Sometimes a truck would come after midnight and we would have to take care of it, unloading. So that was outside my working hours, but I did it to indeed follow his request, not his order or instruction, but his request. For me, I had no limited working hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you do things for him at his home also, not on the business premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When his father would have lumber to be brought into his house, I would go and do it. I wasn't supposed to do that, but I did it. I wasn't supposed to go to the restaurant and bring goods to him to clean his house, to take the garbage out. He asked me to do it and I did it. Actually, I was supposed to officially work in the shop and not in the restaurant or with Miro's father, but I did everything he asked me to. Not just me, Cipeta did the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us where the name Zenga came from? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning I didn't know it, but Zenga is an abbreviation of a Zbor Narodne Garde. These were the first military units that were defending Croatia's independence against the JNA aggression. And Cipeta would start using Zenga, this nickname, when referring to me. Even Miro used this nickname not being aware of what it stood for. It was a joke between Cipeta and myself and people took it up and everybody started calling me Zenga. And now about 80 per cent of the people in my town know me through my nickname Zenga and not my real name, particularly the younger generation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So did Cipeta begin calling you that name because of your experience in Western Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I started calling him Houseman and he started calling me Zenga. His nickname, however, didn't stick to him, but mine did. First the waiters in the restaurant would start calling me Zenga and, you know, when waiters start calling you with this nickname, the guests would and the nickname would just spread around.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now I want to go to the beginning of the war in Konjic. Were you working for Miro during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for Miro up until the beginning of June, 1992, when the war already broke out. Throughout that period I was working for Miro and the first I heard the first grenades, I felt the first shelling. The shells fell on the Ministry of Interior in the area where the office stood, as well as the restaurant, the shop, Miro's shop. The shelling began. We experienced it. We felt the air pressure and we fell. This was a densely built up area. We felt this air pressure. I fell along a wall and Cipeta fell in a garden. The other time we were in the cellar, Miro's cellar of the shop where we hid and later on shelling occurred again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning of the war, were there refugees coming into Konjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am not sure, but I believe that Miro and his restaurant organised food free of charge for refugees. I remember they'd come and eat there. I don't know whether they had to pay. And Cipeta and I, we had to work extra long hours. We had to get additional food supplies. And even the first armed groups in the city were offered food free of charge in that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, in April and May of 1992, were these refugees pouring in from Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the first refugees were coming from Eastern Herzegovina, Nevesinje, the neighbouring Municipality from Konjic, Nevesinje, Gacko and after that from East Bosnia, from Foca and then from the Konjic area, from villages that were burned down by Serbs. So you had also these refugees coming in. Quite a number. They were housed in some collective centres in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when these refugees came into Konjic, what kind of stories did they bring to the residents of the Konjic Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I often heard stories. Mainly, when they'd come to Miro's restaurant, these were women with children. It's -- that they told us that the men were immediately killed on the spot. That women were often raped; girls, 15, 16-years-old, so you heard these stories. I heard that day in and day out. And also, the waiters would begin to talk to them, who these people are. They would ask where they come from. Then Cipeta and I would be helping there and we would be listening to these stories. And, in the city, I could see them coming. You could see groups of refugees coming in, carrying their belongings in plastic bags, so you have these pictures and situations you could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And these tales of horrors that these refugees brought to Konjic, what impact did that have on the people of Konjic, on you and your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an example, I will tell you a situation. On the other side of the road of my ex-former school, there were three national parties. I had history classes in 1990 about the cases of the Second World War. There was near the school, there was a cafe where Serbs would congregate. And I could hear during history classes, we could hear that they were singing Chetnik songs and also wearing such insignia. They were shooting in the air and so on while we were listening to history classes and lessons and the pupils were afraid. And once the refugees were coming in, we expected that Konjic would face the same fate. We expected such a fate for Konjic also. Thank god this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about right next to your secondary school, you heard Chetnik songs. Exactly what does that mean? Because a lot of people don't know that the background of Chetnik songs versus the Ustasha, et cetera, in World War II, what did that mean to you sitting in a history class?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the text of these songs. I never knew these songs. But, later on, I have seen and read these texts. And these songs sing about killing and slaughter. They say, who says that Serbia is small? It's not small. It's fought three times and if need be, it will fight again. So really these songs are an invitation to fight. People were afraid to sleep at home in their respective homes. We set up guards in front of the houses. We were afraid people would come and kill, kill our women and there was a lot of fear, fear among refugees, fear amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back to your history class and these Chetnik songs. That happened in early of 1991, before you went to work for Miro, before you got your JNA notice? Is that when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was still going to school, the moment the national parties won the elections and that occasion, then there was more freedom for those nationalistic-oriented individuals. And some of these people wore openly - carried weapons, pistols, even rifles. And so we had Serbs. There were about half Serbs and it was difficult to control them. For example, in the evening, you come home, you hear in the evening, shooting from restaurants, bombs were thrown. And the police couldn't control that. And what the police did do, then the party leaderships tried to resolve that in another way and these people were released the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did the first shelling of Konjic actually begin sometime in May? When was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I know that the first shells fell, the cemetery is Muslim and the Catholic cemetery. I know that they wanted to shoot at the office of the Ministry of the Interior. But it's a densely built up area where some 50 per cent of the population is Muslim. And the first shells fell into the Muslim cemetery and the Catholic one. I remember that, but I don't know exactly the date, beginning of May, probably, but I cannot say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, after the shelling started, were you still working for Miro in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, up until the month of June. But the shelling was going on, heavy shelling was going on even prior to my leaving Miro. I worked for Miro, I knew that barracks in Ljuta were occupied. This was all happening. I heard about that. I heard that Bradina was liberated. That the barracks in Ljuta were occupied and so on. I heard all these stories from people who were coming to lunch at Miro's restaurant. And, all the time, I was working for Miro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In the beginning, the first resistance was formed in Miro's restaurant, with who? Who helped form the first resistance? And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Asaf and some other -- I knew some other people from Prkanj, people who would be meeting at night in Miro's restaurant. I wasn't personally in the restaurant, Cipeta and myself, we would be in guarding, standing guard in front of the restaurant in order to be able to see if anybody was coming. But I didn't know most of these people. I saw them in uniforms and with weapons at night. But, in daytime, they weren't in uniforms, but only at night they'd organise themselves in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: By Asaf, do you refer to Asaf Jusufovic who came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have known him a long, long time. He had a small dog that was following him everywhere. That's why I knew the man. We knew him as Asaf, but I didn't know the sir name. I knew him as Asaf and I knew his brother, Ahmet Aziz.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would it be safe to say that a lot of military action was beginning to take place in the Konjic area in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the period when I was listening that activities were going on in Donje Selo. And I heard about the barracks being occupied. I even believe that a person from Prkanj was severely injured when fighting in the area of Prkanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: With all of this action, military action and planning and resistance being organised, during that time, did you feel left out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. As a young person, I am sure that also many other young people wanted to contribute to the defence of our country. It was our duty as the inhabitant citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We didn't want our mothers and sisters to happen what happened to these refugees. And Miro told me to sign up to the TO, Territorial Defence, which had its headquarters in the Ministry of Interior. They didn't want to accept me because they said I was too young. That was one of their commanders who said it. He told me, kid, what are you doing here? Get out. I wanted to sign up for the service and I was excluded. Later on, I tried to sign up again and later on I did at the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll have to break here and reassemble at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. McHenry -- Ms. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But Ms. McHenry is back. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, we had just, I think, gotten up to where you were about to join the TO. Can you tell me the circumstances of how you were finally able to join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning of June I was still working for Miro. I was at his place, the place where his father lived, but his father and mother already were evacuated. So, I helped Miro with all the housework and everything he needed. Once I went shopping and I met a friend, a friend of mine, and he was in uniform and bearing arms, had arms. And he said he had signed up for the TO the next day, the next day they would be leaving for some place. Then I went back to Miro's and I informed him that I would like to sign up. But he insisted that I stay. He told me, you're too young, this isn't a war for you, you're too young for that, it's for nobody, no wise person. But it was stronger than me. And it's the only time that I refused what he wanted from me. I went to sign up on the right side of the Neretva River where my parents lived, and that is where I signed up. And some two or three days later I was sent to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you say you signed up for the Territorial Defence, what was the status of your father and your two brothers at that point, or three brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father was involved from the beginning, he was the street guard with my brother and then he signed up for the TO. And my father also told me that it would be wise to join, because I was, it would be my duty. And in my understanding, I thought I really had to join in, and that's what I did, with the advice of my father, advice of my friends. But Miro was against it. But I'm sorry I didn't listen to him on that occasion. I'm sorry that was my biggest mistake for not listening to him on that occasion. Soon after that he left as a refugee, and certainly it would have been better for me to listen to him than it turned out, as I didn't listen to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you joined the TO, I think you said that was the first part of June sometime, when was it, exactly, that you were sent to Celebici, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was somewhere on the 15th, or 17th of June that I was sent to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you go to Celebici with another group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a full bus load of us, I don't know whether 30 or 40 people, but the bus was full of soldiers. A bus of a medium size, there were people from different units, but all under the command of the right side of the bank of Neretva. Some of them I did know and others I didn't. There were some people from my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say under the control of the right side of the Neretva River, would that have been Captain Kazazic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what rank he had at that time, but we called him commander, a commander of the right bank, but I really don't know his rank at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you were sent to Celebici, what were you told before you went to Celebici? What were you expecting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first superior commander, I believe a Croat, I don't remember his name, but he was from my neighbourhood. He told me and all of us would be going to Celebici in order to guard a military facility because in that facility we would be setting up a training camp for the young soldiers, and that after that we would return to Konjic. But we didn't have an clue that it, there was a prison for the rebellious Serbs. I thought I would be guarding a military facility where young soldiers would undergo their training.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And how long were you in Celebici before you realised they were holding detainees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that the second day after coming, but I found out that the first day when I came, I found out that it was a prison, a camp. Maybe a year or a month, an hour or two after coming, and I saw them personally, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, when you were stationed at Celebici, what was your task? What were your duties, as the young guards, or as the young soldiers who just arrived in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was only a guard and to obey orders, to guard, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And were you given your duties at that point, or did you go through some kind of, some kind of training or some kind of indoctrination into Celebici when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When we were leaving from Konjic by bus, we arrived to the barracks of Celebici, we entered the gates, and the bus stopped, we stopped at the gate, we went out and we were told to line up into lines. After that, Pavo Mucic arrived from the command headquarters, he introduced himself, he chose 20 soldiers in full uniform with arms, real soldiers, and to the rest he told to mount the bus and go back from where they came from. After that we were told where we would, our living quarters would be; that was the half warehouse, half where we would be sleeping. And after half an hour's time or maybe an hour after leaving our things Pavo called us out in the field. We sat down on the grass, he chose Sejo Mustafic to be the commander of the guards, we turned to him, if we need anything for any explanation he explained our duties and our obligations as guards and what is to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, can you stand up and point on the model in front of you where the bus stopped, where the young soldiers were lined up, and then once half were chosen where they were told to sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus stopped here (indicating). The bus stopped here (indicating). Here we lined up. INTERPRETER: I'm sorry, we cannot hear him at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Mr. Mucic came to the two lines. After that we were sent to the building D, where would be our living quarters. Then we congregated in front of that building, and Mr. Mucic explained our duties or obligations, and he also said that, who the commander of the guards would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what were your duties and obligations that were explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we come here to be guards, and to carry out all the tasks without any resistance. And he told us it's not to think, but to do and to execute what is being ordered. And that is something which was repeated many times. If we tried to ask something, it's not, we were told, it's not up to you to think, but it's up to you to do and to work. We were told that the detainees were the Chetniks who were taken in prison from Donje Selo from Bradina, that we must be very careful in our contacts with them, that they could take our weapons, they might shoot a guard or all guards, that there can - nobody can enter the barracks, the camp without permission. These were the general type of information which we received, and that weren't to ask and also that we are to execute orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, these young guards that were now assigned these guard duties to, who were explained to you were dangerous detainees, had these young guards had military experience before? We know you hadn't, but had the other young guards had military experience before, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, well, some 25 of us remained, and I would say maybe six or seven adults, as I believe had served their military service in the JNA. Others were all young people from my neighbourhood and the town, maybe a year older or a year younger than I was. So, mainly younger people. And I really don't know why they chose us. Why they chose these very young people. I believe that they should have chosen more experienced people, older people, people who know something of life, and not young people who have no experience of life. This is what I say now, when I think of it in, as a mature person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, when you first got there, the second day were you assigned any specific duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was assigned to be a guard. I believe that Mustafic Sejo determined which guard - where we would be guarding. The gates there are three guard posts, at the hangar. There is a number of posts, guard posts, or we were sent in patrol along the entire perimeter, within the wired perimeter. There were also dogs there which remained still from the JNA, and we continued to feed these dogs. We did everything that was needed and what was requested. The control and guarding of the entire perimeter and over the various points in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Over the time that you were there, were you assigned one position more than any other position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And could you stand up, and on the model show where you were positioned most of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent most of the time at hangar number 6, near the wired fence, and later on there was a bunker.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the guard post where also other guards would stay when we would change shifts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you make him repeat it? Because they said they did not hear him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, can you repeat that answer about where you were stationed in front of hangar 6 most of the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He can stay seated and repeat it so we will hear everything he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beginning, the first few days or a week, two guards were in, near the fence vis-à-vis hangar number 6, and here we were looking direct at the doors of hangar 6. And then I was on this mound, a new guard post, where I stayed and where other guards would be staying at their shift. And then a machine gun was set up there. Often there were people in the village who would be shooting, and they would be shooting at the hangar, at the camp. And that is why that guard point was set up, in order to defend it if anybody tried to enter it by force. From that first guard point it wasn't possible to control well the hangar. We couldn't see who was really entering. The guard -- I'm speaking of the guard point number 1, which you cannot see here on the model.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you said guard point number 1, you can't see it on the model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is that where the machine gun was set up facing the door of hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A ditch was dug, we had a lot of problems when it was raining, it was always full of water, but we always had to stay there. It looked directly into the hangar door, and from the beginning a machine gun was set there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the dugout on top of the hill there, that was your idea, to create that dugout, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I was ordered to be in that guard post, I was always sitting there on the, in the field; but you know, if a car passed, or some drunken soldiers passed by, they could shoot me. That's why I asked Mr. Delic that we should do something. He told me I could dig a ditch, that I could ask two or three detainees to help me. They were, in fact, doing the work, I was on guard. I even asked Mr. Delic to give additional food rations to these detainees from our portions, and for the work they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, these dugouts up there that you created, did you make those comfortable and put a bed in there, did you outfit them to suit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did a lot there. Often it happened that in our premises we couldn't find a bed, and the other places it was too cold, and often, due to my health problems, I couldn't shift constantly from cold to hot and vice versa, and that is why I set all this up.
