And I could sleep from there, I could be on duty there. This was a dugout made of two parts; the guard would be sitting and watching while I would be sleeping. And the guard who was off duty could go there and sleep there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, even when you were off duty, not guarding, assigned to guard hangar number 6, you still slept in the dugout; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And even when off duty I would sleep there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you also make a house there for your dog?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was-- yes, some two metres from this dugout, a small dog house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And there are two holes there, were they connected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was there. There wasn't -- there was only one hole. I don't know when that was done. Maybe it was dug out later on when I left the camp. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, the dugout that you created was to offer you protection and security at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, that's the only reason I made it. And, of course, very often it would happen that I wouldn't find a free bed to sleep in, so I put these two things together, my daytime premises and my sleeping area. Of course, I had to be given permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you were at, guarding the door of hangar 6, how did the detainees inside communicate if they needed something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember whether this was the situation from the very beginning, but for a period of time two detainees, some sort of orderlies, people in charge of order and communications between the detainees and the guards, they would spend almost the entire day outside until some 10 p.m. And should the detainee want to ask a guard or need something else, he or she would have to address the orderly, the orderly would then contact the guard. That was when I was on duty. What was the situation when I was not there, I do not know. You know, there were all sorts of guards, there were many changes, some of them would come and stay five, seven days and then would leave. I don't know how they operated during their duty service. I did what I was told to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, what you're describing is there were representatives of the detainees who were nominated from inside that made contact with the guards if they needed something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Delic appointed them. These were suitable persons. I don't know why, maybe he knew them, but basically these were two fine individuals. I very often talked to them in a friendly manner, and my assumption is that somebody, perhaps Mr. Delic or Mr. Mucic appointed them. I just know that they were in charge of keeping the order. They couldn't appoint them from among the detainees, neither could this be done by the guards. So, somebody from the management of the camp had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what were the names of the two representatives of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was Cecez Nenad the second was Benja Davor. I think that often there was another one who would join them, but I cannot recall the name. I think that often a third person which joined the company would spend longer periods of time outside. There was somebody called Ceric who was working in a car paint shop before the war. I know that his family name was Ceric. He had workshop, was it paint shop or was it a car mechanic shop, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So did these representatives of the detainees get better treatment? Did they get other privileges that the regular detainees didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can just tell you about my attitude towards them. I don't know how other guards treated them. I tried to observe the instructions and the rules we were told to follow. Of course they were treated in a better way because we were very often in contact with them. They, however, were equal to me. I couldn't differentiate them from the detainees inside. The only difference was that I was in contact with these representatives more frequently, so I could sort of create an opinion about them. But, you know, maybe apart from these two people, who I was in contact with more frequently, the others were sort of a threat to me. But there was really no basic difference between them. I just knew that they were detainees. I was a guard, it was my duty to be there. Sometimes, perhaps, I would talk to them. Perhaps I would establish a closer contact with these two than with the others, so this was just the result of the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, when you say sometimes you were afraid of the detainees inside Hangar 6 at night-time, were there two guards guarding 250 to 300 detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not just at night, round the clock. There were always two guards and, for example, let me tell you when we arrived there. We had very old rifles, calibre 48, with five rounds. And two of us had to guard this large number of detainees. At that time, we didn't know that an entire wall of the hangar could be opened up. And you can imagine what could have happened had the detainees opened this large gate. Had we known that, we would be even more afraid than we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, for someone who is not an weapons expert like myself, when you say you were two guards guarding 300 detainees with two old rifles with so many rounds, how many bullets did you have between you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had five bullets in my rifle. He had five bullets in his rifle. And we each had an additional set of five bullets. So a total of twenty. And these were repeat guns, so once you had fired a bullet, you would have to repeat it. And have 250 people running out of the hangar, I would have no time to repeat the round. You know, it's just a matter of a few seconds for these people to cover three, four metres. They needed only a few seconds from the hangar to reach us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say repeat, are you talking about you would have to cock the gun again or something like that before it would fire again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's like hunting shotguns, once you have fired the bullet, the shell has to be ejected, then you have to cock it again and fire and so on. So it's just like a hunting gun, shotgun, but this was a very old military rifle that used to be in use in the past.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, going back to these representatives of the detainees, did those two people that were the representatives, did they go and get the food and distribute the food to the detainees themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- well, I know him, how he looks like. I only --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you to describe a person. I asked you if the representatives were the ones who went to get the food for the detainees and if the representatives were the ones who distributed the food to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not always. There were also other persons that went to fetch the food. And these two individuals sometimes distributed the food. Sometimes they did go and fetch the food and help in the distribution. But, as far as I recall, they usually sent out two other or one other detainee to fetch the food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So it was someone from inside Hangar 6 that got the food and brought it back and distributed it, it wasn't one of the guards, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the guards, the guards would not bring the food. It was done by the detainees. The guard would only follow these individuals from Hangar 6 to the headquarters and back because they couldn't be left to walk around alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just to clarify the situation, you arrived in Celebici on around June 15th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when did you leave Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of July, maybe the last week -- the last week of July, 26th, 27th of July. One or two weeks after the Bradina murders, the murder of the military policemen, something around that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, now I want to go to some counts in the indictment that you were charged with and I am going to ask you about the person by name, and, at that point, I would like for you to explain what you know happened to these people, okay? Let's talk about Counts 1 and 2 of the indictment. There is a murder of a person named Scepo Gotovac. What do you know about Mr. Gotovac and when do you think it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to give you the picture of this person. I think this is somebody who was blamed to have killed a Muslim or some Muslims during the Second World War. I think that's the person you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't know, you're going to have to tell me what happened to him, if you remember. Or you're going to have to tell the Trial Chamber, excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know many people, how they look like, but as far as their names are concerned, it's very difficult for me to recall them because you would have 20, 30 people with the same family name. Sometimes you had two, three persons with the same first name. Now, if I knew who this person exactly was, I could tell you what happened to him. I think that's the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you look at the indictment and recount to him the second sentence of the death, then he might remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Gotovac was the one in the indictment where they claim an SDS badge was pinned on his forehead. Would that help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. That's the person who was blamed to have killed two Muslims during the Second World War. Yes, I know that. I wish to apologise, Your Honours, but it's difficult for me to recall the names. I can recall the events, but the names I cannot really. I know, sometime in June, I think, this person was brought to the camp. At that time, I was not on duty, I had a few hours free. I was sitting on the doorstep in front of the headquarters building when this individual was brought in. As far as I can recall it, he was first brought into the sanitation unit. That is, he was put against the wall of this unit, this facility. He had --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me, since we don't know what the sanitation unit was, would you either point to it or describe it to us, so we have a better picture of what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the infirmary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Allow him to conclude, then you can go back for specific places which you did not understand. Let him tell you what he remembers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was just trying to clarify it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're interrupting the trend of his thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, I'll try not to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Building C on this model. He was standing in front of this building for 45 minutes. His name and other information were put down. I know that they took away from him a knife that was hanging around his belt. It had an inscription, Kiseljak Busovaca and a year. And I asked Mr. Delic if I could have the knife. He allowed me to have this knife and this knife at a later time was given to an Arab TV crew. I don't know why this was done. But then, this person was taken to Hangar 6. After a period of time, I saw him in front of the headquarters' buildings -- well, an old man came. I saw him often walking along the barbed wire. We called him Father Huso. He came and asked for the warden. And I know that he was talking through the window to them in the office where Delic and Mucic were sitting. Then he went into the office. I don't know what they talked about in the office, some ten fifteen minutes later, Delic asked me to go come to the window. I arrived there and I saw Mucic, Delic and Boric and this old man. They were sitting, they were drinking and I think that Mucic wrote down the name of this new detainee on a piece of paper. He gave it to Delic and Delic gave it to me. And Delic then told me, tomorrow I want to see this individual with his feet forward at the gate to the camp and I don't care how you're going to do it. That was during the day. That was the order to me. During the night, I, together with some three, four other guards, I called out this individual to go out of the hangar because I was given an order. I was expected to submit a report subsequently whether I have executed the order or not. So I took this person out of the hangar, the five of us, I think. We would beat this person. We would kick them. Somebody kick him with a rifle butt, well, you know, it was dark, it was difficult to see. And this area was not lit, so, sometimes, we guards would kick each other. After about half an hour, I brought this person back. I know that he was alive when I took him back. I went back to Mr. Delic. I told him that the order has been executed. In the morning I was told that the man was dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you called him out, you went to the door of Hangar 6 and called Mr. Scepo Gotovac to come out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then when you say he was beaten by four or five guards, that means each one of them were under the orders to carry out this order?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, good afternoon. I would like to object to the continued leading of Defence counsel, including to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. His evidence was clear, the instruction was given to him, not to the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, then, how did the other guards come to participate in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somebody sent them, perhaps they were ordered too, I don't know. When I went out to execute the order, they joined me. They said that they had been ordered to do it. Whether they had been ordered or told to do it, I don't know. But we -- I was ordered, I know that, that this man should go through the gate with his feet forward, which meant that he was to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you took Mr. Gotovac back to the hangar, did you put him inside or did you have help putting him inside? How did he get back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He walked. He was bent a little, so I held him. I think that another guard helped him to take him back, but he could walk back. Since, during night, we were prohibited to enter the hangar, we opened the door, he would make two or three steps forward, then, I think, he sat down. It was dark, I don't know exactly, so we closed the door. And the next day I was told that a detainee died. My assumption was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get the rest of the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The sentence was not finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you escorted Mr. Gotovac back into Hangar No. 6, did he have anything on his forehead at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, let me tell you this. We, when we were given the order to do something, to beat somebody up or anything else, the order was clear that, in any event, whether we should beat them to death or just beat them, that they should not be kicked at their head, so that there would be no bruises on their head. So there was no possibility for anyone to hurt the head. No way. So all the injuries were afflicted on the body. I don't know why this was the order we were given, but we were given this order and we would obey it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you place an SDS badge on Mr. Gotovac's head or did you see anybody else place one on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally didn't. But everything is possible. It's dark, you have five, six people who are beating up him. Maybe somebody did it, I don't know, I cannot tell you this. But I know that I personally didn't do it. Whether somebody else did it, I don't know. It's possible. There is a possibility, everything is possible. I don't really know it. I just know that I didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you said that you all were forbidden to go into the hangar after dark in Hangar 6. What is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably to avoid the detainees attacking the guards, I don't know, that's my assumption. But I know that the order was that we can only open a door for a detainee to go in or out, but we shouldn't ever enter the hangar. There was no light in the hangar, so no guard during the night would go into this hangar. And I was told that that Hangar No. 9 also was not lit and that guards were not supposed to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you have been afraid to go in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Well, when you have 250 people inside, you enter alone, you don't know what can happen. You can expect that from each detainee, that they will try to escape, particularly at a time of war. And there have been cases of attacks on guards. There have been attempts to escape. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to Count No. 5 and 6 in the indictment. Did you know a Serbian man named Simo Jovanovic? I mean a Bosnian man of Serbian decent named Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know him prior to the war. But later on, I heard that he lived in my street, but I didn't know him. Only when he died, I knew who the man was from where he came. I was on guard one night and a group of guards came, who came from the Village of Idbar, Newgarde (Phoen), and Simo also originally came from there. He had a family home there with a big farm. These guards came. And before coming to the hangar, I was on that small mount and told me that I should call out Simo Jovanovic because they wanted to talk to him. There were two guard positions. The guard on the mount would communicate with the detainees and the other guard always had to be present at the machine gun if more detainees try to exit by force. I asked them why they wanted to see the man. They said they had an order to talk to him. I called the man. I couldn't check at that point whether they were ordered to do so or not. There was a telephone, but it was out of order, so I did call him out. They took him and they took him to the hangar workshop, workshop for the repair of weapons. I then went back to my guard position, but I could hear the beating and I could hear the shouts. Some twenty minutes later, one of these came and he said, we finished this Chetnik and we wrote the will. And this was a big man. He was maybe a metre 90. A hefty man. And we really had a lot of trouble to bring him to that hangar. And the next day I heard about it. I don't really know why he was killed. But I did hear later on that his property was divided among the inhabitants. I know that he was beaten that night and that also he died from that beating later that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You say he was taken to the workshop. Could you point on that model where the workshop is? So it would be the hangar next to Hangar No. 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you participate at all in the beating of Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was not ordered to do so. I was on guard duty. I only called him out and accompanied him there. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the position that you always held at the dugout over Hangar 6, is that the position that had along with it the responsibility of communicating with the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That guard from that guard position was to communicate with the detainees because the other guard was always in close proximity of the machine gun, looking directly at the hangar door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: On July 12th, 1992, what happened, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well. Somewhere at 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., I just ended my tour of duty at the point Hangar 6. I came to the command building when Mr. Delic came out of the building and he told me that all guards who are not on duty, that they have to go to Bradina because some policemen were killed by Chetniks. At that point, twelve guards, twelve of us headed by Sejo Mustafic and Buturovic, who was driving the pickup, and we went to Konjic and Podrasac, to the sports field, and Bradina where we were carrying out a field inspection after the killing of these policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you got up to Bradina, or, more specifically, was it a town named Repovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a halfway between the Village of Bradina and Repovci. It was really halfway between the two villages. That's where the killing took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And what did you find when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother at the time was at the military police. I heard that four military policemen were killed in ambush. I was afraid that it might not be my brother. When other military policemen arrived, they mentioned the name of my brother and some other names. And as long as I didn't come to Bradina, I didn't know who was really killed. But then, when I came, I saw who the people who were killed and how they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised all the four military policemen and the other five people accompanying these policemen I didn't know. Aziz Arahmetli, the brother of Jusufovic. I recognised Ive, my neighbour. Then Isak Pandzo, who worked for a certain period of time in Miro's restaurant. And I recognised another neighbour, Zovonimir Pandzo, we called him Pandzo Croat. Those four were killed and five civilians were killed also. Five policemen, a fifth chap who arrived from Germany before the outbreak of the war, both of his ears were cut off after he was killed. I have seen that. There was no blood coming out from these wounds from where his ears were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And in what condition did you find Ibro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even before coming close to that body, I recognised him 120 metres away. His face was turned to the soil, but I recognised him from the body. I fell, I sat down on the road. At that point, I thought I'd prefer my brother to be killed than him. Then I succeeded in getting up. And he had a big hole on his head and many bullet holes in his body, a lot of blood. Then next to him, Aziz, his lower part of the leg was severed. And, under it, Isad Ljeva's body could be observed. I knew him, but he was lying on his shoulders. His mouth was open. His eyes were open, as if he were recognising somebody who was killing him. As if an expression of surprise. And then Pandzo, who, he was lying flat on his belly and he had a wound on his head. And Bato who came from Germany, he was lying on the other side of that van with both ears cut off while the civilians, the penises were cut off. So you could -- bodies were strewn all over the place. 24 25

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you viewed that, were you assigned some specific duty that you were to perform then, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Where, where? In Bradina or in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: There at the scene. You came up there for a purpose, it wasn't just to look at the bodies; what was your purpose for coming up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we came to that place we were inspecting the terrain, and we needed some 45 minutes, we were inspecting the terrain. We were told that the remaining Serbs from Bradina had done this. We inspected the field in order to see were there any traces or any indication. We checked the terrain, and I don't know if anybody else in the other group continued further off. After seeing all of this, we turned back and went to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was Damir Gogic with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the group of members of the military police, and there were people from the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then did you return to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after some spending half an hour at that location we returned to Celebici because we had to take our turns there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And when you were travelling back to Celebici in the truck, was there anything said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, throughout the entire trip back nobody said anything, not a word. We could only see that sad expression of the faces, because we all knew these policemen, everybody was having, was thinking deeply, thinking deeply and nobody uttered a word. It was a shock for all of the people present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you arrived back at Celebici, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived to Celebici in front of the command building, on the window two detainees were cutting bread, preparing it for the dinnertime. And our van stopped, we jumped out and 11 or 12 of us started beating those two detainees. We were beating them for some five minutes, and then Delic took a gun and fired it in the air in order to -- we at that point stopped. It got us out of the shock and we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, a few minutes later I went to hangar number 6, because, you see, I knew of these people, some of my best friends were killed in Bradina. We were told that the Serbs did this from Bradina. I came to that hangar and I told to all the detainees from Bradina to stand up, and when you enter the hangar on the right side I beat, I started beating two, two of them, two of the detainees in order to -- you see, it was to get the anger out, but it wasn't to injure them, and the third or the fourth person I hit, that person fell, fell on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I have to ask you, when you keep saying beating, do you mean you hit them once, twice, for an extended period of time, or was it moving from one to the next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went from one to another of those who were standing up, and I think the first I hit them once, twice, maybe three times each. It's not that I was concentrating on one. I was angry against the people from Bradina. I was told that the Serbs from Bradina killed these policemen. And after hitting them once or twice, each one of them, one of them fell. And I saw as if that person was losing his breath, couldn't breathe. Then I called one of the detainees who earlier worked in Konjic in the hospital, he helped. I know that he was doing something to that man, and he stopped shaking. Then I asked the other two or three detainees and took the man to the infirmary. I wanted really to kill them all, but I didn't have the intention to do anything to that man. Later on I also met his son, and that son told me that this man had earlier cardiac problems, and I hit him once or twice, and that was what then caused these problems. He later on died in the infirmary in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you take him to the infirmary yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, two or three other detainees helped him to the infirmary. They were carrying him in their arms. Maybe, maybe he could have walked, I don't know. So, we took him, carried him. And the doctors tried to do something, tried to help him, but regrettably he died on that day. I don't know exactly what day, but on that day, he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you go to the infirmary to check on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was standing at the entrance door of the infirmary while the doctors were assisting him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And did you tell the doctors anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I said that they should try to help him, to save him. I can't remember exactly the words, but in that I spoke in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you acting under orders at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this is a convenient place to stop, it's really warm in here. I know everybody is probably suffering and we could continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, we can continue tomorrow. We can continue tomorrow morning, 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
